run.name: Fdga Baseline Benchmarks 2601 Congress
run.description: GerryChain ReCom MCMC ensemble — congress redistricting, 99,001 draws across 1 elections.

dem_seats.label: Seat–Vote Proportionality
dem_seats.headline: Does the seat count reflect how people actually voted?
dem_seats.description: In a fair map, the share of seats each party wins should reflect its share of statewide votes. This metric counts districts projected to lean Democratic based on each plan's vote patterns — not as a partisan goal, but as a measuring stick for proportionality. The histogram shows how many Democratic-leaning seats thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. If the enacted map falls far from this range, lines were likely drawn to systematically over- or under-represent one party.
dem_seats.takeaway: The enacted map produces 5 Democratic-leaning seats — at the 46th percentile, within the typical range for neutral maps (median: 6, range: 4–7). No significant seat-count advantage detected for either party.

formula_info.detail: dem_2pv_d = Σ dem_votes_vtd / Σ (dem_votes_vtd + rep_votes_vtd) for all VTDs in district d
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 six-election equal-weight average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov, 2022 Senate, 2024 Pres)

efficiency_gap.label: Wasted Votes Balance
efficiency_gap.headline: Are both parties' votes equally effective at winning representation?
efficiency_gap.description: Every election produces 'wasted' votes — votes cast in losing districts (all wasted) and surplus votes beyond what was needed to win (also wasted). A fair map wastes votes at roughly equal rates for both parties. The Efficiency Gap measures the difference: a positive value means one party's votes are being wasted at a higher rate than the other's — a sign that district lines are concentrating or dispersing that party's voters artificially. Developed by Stephanopoulos & McGhee; cited in federal gerrymandering litigation.
efficiency_gap.takeaway: The enacted map's efficiency gap (0.171) is above the neutral median (0.099), at the 90th percentile — within the normal range for neutral maps. Democratic votes are wasted at a higher rate, giving Republicans a structural advantage in translating votes to seats.

formula_info.formula: (Σ wasted_dem − Σ wasted_rep) / Σ total_votes  across all districts
formula_info.detail: wasted_dem = excess Dem votes beyond 50%+1 in Dem wins + all Dem votes in Dem losses; symmetric for Rep
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 six-election equal-weight average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov, 2022 Senate, 2024 Pres)

mean_median.label: Vote Distribution Symmetry
mean_median.headline: Does each party need the same number of votes to win a district?
mean_median.description: The Mean-Median difference reveals whether one party's votes are systematically spread more efficiently across districts than the other's. When one party wins many districts by modest margins while the other piles up large majorities in fewer districts, the map gives the first party a structural seat advantage — even when both parties receive equal votes statewide. A value near zero means both parties convert votes to seats at roughly the same rate. A large deviation in either direction is a signal of asymmetric voter distribution — often a hallmark of gerrymandering.
mean_median.takeaway: The mean–median difference (0.080) is above the neutral median (0.036), at the 100th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps. Democratic voters are disproportionately concentrated in fewer districts, giving Republicans a more efficient geographic spread of support.

formula_info.detail: Positive → Dem votes distributed less efficiently across districts (Republican structural advantage). Negative → reverse.
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 six-election equal-weight average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov, 2022 Senate, 2024 Pres)

comp_seats_7pt.label: Electoral Competitiveness (7-pt)
comp_seats_7pt.headline: How many districts give voters a meaningful choice?
comp_seats_7pt.description: A competitive district is one where the outcome is genuinely uncertain — where the margin between the two parties is within 5 percentage points of 50/50. Competitive districts force elected officials to be responsive to a broad range of constituents, not just their party base. Maps designed to protect incumbents — whether Republican or Democratic — tend to minimize competitiveness. This metric asks whether the enacted map produces fewer competitive districts than neutral alternatives would.
comp_seats_7pt.takeaway: The enacted map has zero competitive districts within the 5pp threshold. At the 5th percentile, this is toward the edge of the normal range. Every district has a predetermined partisan lean — voters have no meaningful choice in any race.

formula_info.detail: A district is competitive if the two-party Democratic share falls within ±competitive_margin of 50%
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 six-election equal-weight average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov, 2022 Senate, 2024 Pres)

comp_seats_10pt.label: Electoral Competitiveness (10-pt)
comp_seats_10pt.headline: How many districts give voters a meaningful choice?
comp_seats_10pt.description: A competitive district is one where the outcome is genuinely uncertain — where the margin between the two parties is within 5 percentage points of 50/50. Competitive districts force elected officials to be responsive to a broad range of constituents, not just their party base. Maps designed to protect incumbents — whether Republican or Democratic — tend to minimize competitiveness. This metric asks whether the enacted map produces fewer competitive districts than neutral alternatives would.
comp_seats_10pt.takeaway: The enacted map has just 2 competitive district(s) — fewer than 81% of neutral maps. Most voters live in districts where outcomes are predetermined.

formula_info.detail: A district is competitive if the two-party Democratic share falls within ±competitive_margin of 50%
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 six-election equal-weight average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov, 2022 Senate, 2024 Pres)

dem_safe_seats.label: Safe Democratic Seats
dem_safe_seats.headline: How many districts lean solidly Democratic — beyond the competitive margin?
dem_safe_seats.description: Counts districts where the Democratic two-party vote share exceeds 50% + 5pp — the outer boundary of the competitive zone. These seats are reliably Democratic and not meaningfully contested. Together with safe Republican seats and competitive seats, this completes the three-bucket political balance picture from the scorecard. An unusually high or low count signals packing or cracking of Democratic voters relative to what neutral geography-driven redistricting would produce.
dem_safe_seats.takeaway: Enacted value: 5.000. Neutral median: 5.000 (range: 4.000–6.000). At the 79th percentile — within the normal range for neutral maps.

formula_info.detail: Democratic-leaning districts outside the competitive zone — margin exceeds threshold on the Democratic side

rep_safe_seats.label: Safe Republican Seats
rep_safe_seats.headline: How many districts lean solidly Republican — beyond the competitive margin?
rep_safe_seats.description: Counts districts where the Republican two-party vote share exceeds 50% + 5pp — the outer boundary of the competitive zone. These seats are reliably Republican and not meaningfully contested. Together with safe Democratic seats and competitive seats, this completes the three-bucket political balance picture from the scorecard. An unusually high or low count signals packing or cracking of Republican voters relative to what neutral geography-driven redistricting would produce.
rep_safe_seats.takeaway: Enacted value: 9.000. Neutral median: 6.000 (range: 4.000–8.000). At the 100th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps.

formula_info.detail: Republican-leaning districts outside the competitive zone — margin exceeds threshold on the Republican side

maj_black.label: Black Demographic Majority Districts
maj_black.headline: How does the map distribute districts with a Black demographic majority?
maj_black.description: Counts districts where Black Citizen Voting Age Population (CVAP) meets or exceeds the selected threshold. At 50% (default): districts where Black citizens constitute a majority of eligible voters. Slide the threshold down to 20% to see districts where Black voters hold meaningful but not majority electoral weight. The histogram shows how many districts at the selected threshold thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. Symmetric grading: both unusually high and unusually low counts relative to the neutral ensemble signal that district boundaries depart from what geography and demographics alone would produce. Uses 2024 ACS CVAP Special Tabulation (any-part Black Citizen VAP / Total Citizen VAP). CVAP excludes non-citizen population from the denominator.
maj_black.takeaway: The enacted map has 5 majority-Black district(s) — above 99% of neutral maps (neutral range: 1–3). This is a statistical outlier: well above what geography and demographics alone would typically produce.

formula_info.detail: Uses 2024 ACS CVAP Special Tabulation (any-part Black CVAP / Total Citizen VAP), aggregated to 2020 VTDs by build_cvap_vtd.py. CVAP excludes non-citizen population from the denominator, so Black-majority districts correctly show 51-57% rather than 47-49%.
formula_info.data_source: 2024 ACS CVAP Special Tabulation (any-part Black CVAP / Total Citizen VAP) — cvap_vtd.parquet
formula_info.grading_method: symmetric (both tails notable — unusually high or low deviates from neutral geography)

maj_white.label: Majority-White Districts
maj_white.headline: How many districts have a white-citizen majority of eligible voters?
maj_white.description: Counts districts where non-Hispanic white Voting Age Population meets or exceeds the selected threshold. At 50% (default): districts with a true white-citizen majority of eligible voters. Slide the threshold down to 20% to see districts where white voters hold strong but not majority influence. Shown alongside Black and Minority Coalition metrics to complete the full demographic picture of how the map distributes political power across racial groups. The Princeton ensemble test grades statistical distance from neutral redistricting outcomes symmetrically — unusually high or low counts compared to neutral maps both indicate the map departs from geography-driven redistricting.
maj_white.takeaway: The enacted map has 9 majority-white district(s), within the typical range for neutral maps (8–11).

formula_info.detail: Districts where non-Hispanic white citizens are a majority of eligible voters (2020 Census P0040005). Shown alongside minority metrics to complete the demographic picture.

min_coal.label: Minority Coalition Majority Districts
min_coal.headline: How does the map distribute districts with a non-white demographic majority?
min_coal.description: Counts districts where non-white Voting Age Population meets or exceeds the selected threshold. At 50% (default): districts where communities of color collectively constitute a majority of eligible voters. At 20%: broader districts where diverse communities have meaningful but not majority electoral weight. Symmetric grading: both unusually high and unusually low counts relative to the neutral ensemble indicate that district boundaries depart from what geography and demographics alone would produce. Uses 2024 ACS CVAP Special Tabulation (non-white Citizen VAP / Total Citizen VAP).
min_coal.takeaway: The enacted map has 5 minority-coalition district(s) — above the typical neutral range (3–6), at the 95th percentile.

formula_info.detail: Combined non-white VAP share (1 − NH White fraction). A minority-coalition district includes multiple racial groups, none individually a majority.
formula_info.grading_method: symmetric (both tails notable — unusually high or low deviates from neutral geography)

min_influence.label: Minority Influence Districts
min_influence.headline: How many districts have a significant but sub-majority minority population?
min_influence.description: Counts districts where communities of color collectively hold between the FDGA influence floor (37%) and the majority threshold (50%) of the Citizen Voting Age Population. These districts have a significant minority presence — enough to meaningfully influence electoral outcomes — without constituting a demographic majority. More influence districts indicates broader minority electoral participation across the map. Both thresholds are configurable.
min_influence.takeaway: The enacted map has 3 minority influence district(s) — fewer than 98% of neutral maps (typical range: 4–8). Communities of color have fewer districts where they can meaningfully influence electoral outcomes than neutral redistricting would typically produce.

formula_info.detail: Districts where communities of color collectively hold between the lower influence floor and the majority threshold of Citizen Voting Age Population — above the level where minority voters can meaningfully influence electoral outcomes, but below a demographic majority.

muni_splits.label: Split Cities & Municipalities
muni_splits.headline: How many cities and towns are divided across different districts?
muni_splits.description: Counts incorporated municipalities (cities, towns) whose territory is split across two or more congressional districts. Urban cracking — dividing a city among multiple districts — dilutes its collective political voice and reduces the ability of city residents to elect a single representative who understands local concerns. Fewer splits means more communities are kept intact. The neutral ensemble shows how many splits geography-driven redistricting would typically produce; the enacted map is compared against this baseline.
muni_splits.takeaway: The enacted map splits just 12 cities and municipalities — fewer than 100% of neutral maps (typical range: 21–34). Urban communities are exceptionally well preserved compared to what neutral redistricting would produce.

formula_info.formula: count(municipalities m : ∃ VTDs v1, v2 ∈ m assigned to different districts)
formula_info.detail: An incorporated municipality (city, town) is 'split' when at least two of its VTDs are assigned to different districts. Urban cracking indicator.
